1.x: The transition from “praying for workers” to “sending workers” is completed. Jesus moves from a solo ministry to a delegated one, officially forming the leadership structure of the early Church. He calls twelve disciples. The number twelve is highly symbolic. Just as there were twelve tribes of Israel in the OT, Jesus is establishing twelve apostles to represent the “New Israel.” Jesus “gave them power.” The disciples aren’t working based on their own talent or training; they are operating on delegated authority. Notice “forgiving sins” is not part of the authority they’re given. Only God can forgive sins (Ps 51:1-2; 32:5;25:11;Lk 11:4; 23:34; Mt 6:12;1 Jn 1:9; Acts 8:22). Men do not have authority to forgive sins against God’s Law. Men can only forgive sins committed against their personal person (Lk 11:2-4;17:3-4; Mt 18:21-22). The false religions that teach that priests have the authority from God to forgive sins on demand use John 20:21-23 as “evidence”. See notes on John 20:21-23 for a proper breakdown of the verse in context.

2.x: Disciple means “learner” or “follower.” Apostle means “one who is sent” or “ambassador.” The Apostles have moved from being students in the classroom to representatives in the field. Matthew makes a subtle but important change in terminology here. The apostles in v.2 are: (1) Simon, called Peter: a fisherman from Bethsaida (later living in Capernaum) along with his brother Andrew. Jesus renamed him “Peter” (meaning “rock” or “stone”, not a “bedrock” nor a “foundational rock’). After making his confession of faith, he is the first to be given the keys of heaven (Mt 16:19). The rest of the apostles get this same authority in Mt 18:18. Peter was part of Jesus’ inner circle (with James and John) and witnessed the Transfiguration, the raising of Jairus’ daughter, and the agony in Gethsemane. He is known for his bold (and sometimes impulsive) personality. He was the first to confess Jesus as the Messiah, walked on water briefly, denied Jesuss three times, but was restored after the resurrection (Jn 21:15-19). He became a leader in the early church (preaching at Pentecost in Acts 2, performing miracles, and opening the gospel to Gentiles in Acts 10). He wrote the books of 1-2 Peter. (2) Andrew (Peter’s brother): Also a fisherman; he was originally a disciple of John the Baptist and one of the first to follow Jesus (Jn 1:35-42). He brought his brother Peter to Jesus and later introduced others (like the boy with the loaves and fishes in Jn 6). He is often associated with humble service and evangelism. (3) James (son of Zebedee), also called James the Greater: Fisherman and brother of John; part of the inner circle with Peter and John. Jesus nicknamed him and John “Sons of Thunder” (Boanerges), likely due to their fiery zeal (like wanting to call down fire on a Samaritan village in Lk 9:54). He was the first apostle to be martyred, beheaded by King Herod Agrippa around 44AC (Acts 12:1-2). (4) John (brother of James the Great): Fisherman; also part of the inner circle and often called “the disciple whom Jesus loved” in his own Gospel. He is present at key events: the Transfiguration, the Last Supper (leaning on Jesus), the crucifixion (where Jesus entrusted this mother to him), and the empty tomb. He authored the Gospel of John, 1-3 John, and Revelation. John was probably Jesus’ cousin. This comes mainly from two parallel passages: (a) “Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the Less and of Joses, and SALOME;” (b) “his mother, and HIS MOTHER’S SISTER, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene” (Jn 19:25). If “Mary the mother of James the Less and of Joses” is the same as “Mary the wife of Cleophas”, then “Salome” is “[Mary]’s sister,” making John & James the Greater Jesus’ first cousins. This would explain the closeness they both had with Jesus as members of his inner circle.

3.x: (5) Philip: From Bethsaida, like Peter and Andrew. He brought Nathanael (Bartholomew) to Jesus (Jn 1:43-46). In John’s gospel, he appears in several scenes: questioning how to feed the 5,000, asking Jesus to show the Father (Jn 14:8-9), and being approached by Greeks wanting to see Jesus (Jn 12:12-22). Do not confuse “Philip the apostle” and “Philip the deacon” (also called “Philip the evangelist”). Philip the deacon is one of the seven chosen in Acts 6 to serve (diakonia) the widows and the poor in the Jerusalem church (Acts 21:8). He also preaches and performs miracles in Samaria (Acts 8:4-13). And is this Philip that meets and baptizes the Ethiopian eunuch on the road from Jerusalem to Gaza (Acts 8:26-39). Later texts place the deacon living in Caesarea with his four prophesying daughters (Acts 21:8-9). (6) Bartholomew (likely the same as Nathanael): Introduced to Jesus by Philip the apostle. Jesus praised him as “an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit” (Jn 1:47). He witnessed the risen Jesus and was present at the Sea of Galilee appearance (Jn 21). Little else is recorded in the NT. (7) Thomas (also called Didymus, meaning “twin”): Known as “doubting Thomas” for initially refusing to believe the resurrection unless he could see and touch Jesus’ wounds (Jn 20:24-29). Jesus appeared and invited him to do so, leading Thomas to declare: “My Lord and my God!”. He was courageous and loyal. When Jesus planned to go to Judea (where danger awaited), Thomas said: “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (Jn 11:16). (8) Matthew (the tax collector, also called Levi): A tax collector (publican) for the Romans, a despised profession among Jews because of corruption and collaboration with occupiers. Jesus called him while he was at his tax booth (Mt 9:9); Matthew immediately left everything, hosted a feast for Jesus with other “sinners” and became a disciple. He is attributed this gospel, which has a strong Jewish focus and emphasizes how Jesus fulfills the OT prophecy. (9) James (son of Alphaeus), also called James the Less or James the Younger: Distinguished from James son of Zebedee to avoid confusion. Very little is recorded about him personally in the gospels. Catholics try to argue that he is James “the Lord’s brother” in order to maintain Mary’s perpetual virginity. But reading the Bible, notice how every James is differentiated by a family member, and every family member of Jesus is described in relation to Jesus (“his brother”, “his mother”, “the Lord’s brother”, etc). (10) Thaddaeus (also called Judas son of James, Lebbaeus, or Jude - not to be confused with Judas Iscariot or the author of Jude): Listed with alternate names across the gospels (Matthew uses Thaddaeus/Lebbaeus; Luke and Acts use Judas son of James). He asked Jesus a question at the Last Supper: “Lord, how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world?” (Jn 14:22 KJV).

4.x: (11) Simon the Canaanite (or Simon the Zealot): The “zealot” label likely refers to his prior affiliation with the Zealot movement (Jewish nationalists who opposed Roman rule, sometimes violently) or simply his zealous personality. Almost nothing else is recorded about his life or actions in the NT. (12) Judas Iscariot: The only non-Galillean in the group (from Kerioth in Judea - “Iscariot” likely means “man of Kerioth”). He served as the group’s treasurer but was a thief who stole from the moneybag (Jn 12:6). He betrayed Jesus to the chief priests for 30 pieces of silver, identifying him with a kiss in Gethsemane (Mt 26). Overcome with remorse, he returned the money and hanged himself (Mt 27:3-5); Acts 1:18 adds a graphic detail of his death. He was replaced by Matthias (chosen by lot in Acts 1:15-26) to restore the number to twelve.

5.x: These twelve were ordinary men: mostly uneducated fishermen, plus a tax collector and a possible political zealot, whom Jesus chose, trained, and empowered. Despite their flaws (impulsiveness, doubt, denial, betrayal), they formed the foundation of the early church after the resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. Most (except John) are traditionally believed to have been martyred for their faith, spreading the gospel across the known world. However, at this stage, Jesus is focusing on the historical promise: the gospel must first be offered to Israel, the people of the covenant, as the initial step in God’s plan of redemption.

6.x: Jesus is sending his apostles to the very people he felt compassion for: the ones let down by their own religious leadership (the sheep without a pastor of Mt 9:36).

7.x: They are not yet sent to preach the full story of the crucifixion and resurrection (which the disciples themselves do not fully understand yet). Instead, they are to act as “heralds” announcing that the King has arrived and His kingdom is now accessible.

8.x: Jesus is delegating his own miracle-working authority to them. The list covers the full spectrum of suffering: physical illness (the sick), social/ritual impurity (the lepers), mortality (the dead), and spiritual bondage (the devils). The instruction “freely ye have received, freely give” is the foundational principle of Christian ministry. Because the disciples didn’t “earn” this power from Jesus, they are strictly forbidden from charging for it. It is a gift meant to be passed on, not a commodity to be sold.

16.x: This specific mission is often called the “Limited Commission.” It was a training exercise. Jesus was showing them that the power he gave them in verse 1 was enough to sustain them, even if they had nothing else. Sheep are defenseless, gentle, and have no natural way to fight a wolf. Jesus is being brutally honest: they are not going on a vacation, but to a conflict zone where they will be physically and socially vulnerable. Jesus calls for a balance of two traits: (1) Wise as serpents: Don’t be naive. Be cautious, observant, and aware of the traps set by those who oppose the message. (2) Harmless as doves: Don’t be corrupt. Even when under attack, do not retaliate with the same malice or “wolf-like” aggression as your enemies, but rather flee.

17.x: Jesus gives them a “heads up” so they won’t be caught by surprise. The “Councils” refer to the local Sanhedrin (local religious courts) in the towns they visit. The “scourge” was a brutal form of punishment (often 39 lashes) performed inside the synagogues themselves. This shows how deeply religious establishments would reject the message of the Kingdom.

18.x: You might expect Jesus to say they will be brought before leaders to be silenced; instead, he says they are brought there “for a testimony.” What looks like a trial of the disciples is actually a trial of the kings and governors. By appearing before them, the Apostles are forced to bring the message of the Kingdom to the highest levels of government. The “persecuted” become the “witness” to the powerful. An example of this is Paul. God used Peter and other fishermen to bring the gospel to the common people, but He used Paul, an educated man, to share the gospel with high ranking Roman officials, such as: (1) Felix, Roman governor of Judea (Acts 24:10-26); (2) Festus, successor to Felix (Acts 25:8-11;26:24-26); (3) King Agrippa II and Bernice (Roman-client rulers) (Acts 26:2-29); (4) Before Caesar in Rome (Acts 28:30-31).

19.x: “Take no thought”: This doesn’t mean “don’t study” or “be lazy”. In the original Greek, it means “don’t be anxious.” Jesus is telling them not to lose sleep over the legal strategy or the specific wording of their defense. God doesn’t necessarily give the script a week in advance; He provides the words exactly when they are needed.

20.x: Jesus clarifies that the disciple is merely the vessel. The actual “Speaker” in the courtroom is the Holy Spirit. “Spirit of your Father”: By using this phrase, Jesus reminds them of their relationship. A father doesn’t abandon his child in a legal crisis.

Who is giving the words? (1) The Father: “For it is not ye that speak, but the Spirit of your Father which speaketh in you.” (v.20); (2) Jesus: “For I(Jesus) will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist.” (Lk 21:15 KJV); (3) YHWH: “Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say.” (Ex 4:12 KJV); (4) The Holy Spirit: “take no thought beforehand what ye shall speak, neither do ye premeditate: but whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye: for it is not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost.” (Mk 13:11 KJV). From a Oneness point of view, this is very simple: the one who speaks is the one singular masculine divine Spirit. The Bible constantly states that there is only one Spirit: “There is one body(the church), and ONE SPIRIT(God)” (Eph 4:4 KJV) & “For by ONE SPIRIT(God) are we all baptized into one body(the church)...and have been all made to drink into ONE SPIRIT(God)” (1 Cor 12:13 KJV). ONE SPIRIT. Yet, we see: (1) “Spirit of God” (Gen 1:2); (2) “Spirit of the LORD(YHWH)” (Judges 6:34); (3) “Spirit of your Father” (Mt 10:20); (4) “the Holy Spirit” (Jn 14:26); (5) “Spirit of Jesus” (Phil 1:19); (6) “Spirit of Christ” (Rom 8:9), etc. We do not have 6 different Spirits, rather it’s the same Spirit described differently. Some describe His holiness, others His covenant name, His works or His attributes. That is why Peter could say that the Spirit of Christ was the same Spirit working in the prophets of the OT (1 Pet 1:10-11). Dividing the different Spirits into different persons within the Godhead is a terrible mistake that most Trinitarians fall into. God is only one divine person, not three. The Greek does not allow for a multiplicity of persons within the Godhead: “For there is ONE(heis: singular masculine one that demands one person) God, and one mediator between God and men, the MAN(the human born of Mary, not a second divine person) Christ Jesus” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV).

23.x: Jesus explicitly permits “fleeing.” He doesn’t command them to be martyrs if there is a way to escape and continue the mission elsewhere. They are to be “wise as serpents” (v.16), not reckless with their lives. “Till the Son of man be come”: The coming of the Lord is usually tied to judgement. Given the context, it likely refers to Jesus coming in Judgement upon the Israelites during the destruction of the 2nd Temple in Jerusalem 70AC.

26.x: “Feat them not therefore”: This is a direct conclusion based on v.24-25. If the world treats you like it treated Jesus, you are in good company. Fear is often the result of feeling alone or out of control; Jesus reminds them they are following a set path. Jesus says that there will be nothing that won’t be revealed. In the 1st century, religious leaders (like the Pharisees) often operated with “covered” motives; they looked holy on the outside but were full of “dead men’s bones” on the inside. The secret plots, slanders, and private wickedness of the persecutors will eventually be brought into the light of God’s judgement. They will not “get away with it” forever. For the disciples, their message, which at this point is being spoken in small rooms or to “lost sheep” in Galilee, will eventually be broadcast to the entire world. The truth of the gospel cannot remain a secret. Truth is more durable than lies. Jesus is essentially giving them encouragement, telling them that the power of their persecutors is based on a facade that is already crumbling, while the message of the gospel will ultimately stand in the light.

27.x: Jessu takes the principle of “nothing is hidden” from the previous verse and turns it into a direct mandate for the disciples. He is moving them from private training to public proclamation. At this point in Matthew’s gospel, Jesus had often taught his disciples in private or used parables that the general public didn’t fully grasp. Verse 27 makes the “end of the secret.” “In darkness” / “In the ear”: This refers to the intimate, quiet moments of discipleship. Jesus had been whispering the deep truths of the Kingdom into their ears behind closed doors. “In light”/”Upon the housetops”: In 1st-century Judea, houses had flat roofs. These were often used as public squares or platforms for making announcements to the neighborhoods. Jesus is telling them to take the private revelations he gave them and broadcast them as loudly and publicly as possible. This verse is a direct follow-up to the command “Fear them not” (v.26). Jesus is telling them to refuse to hide (acting like a secret society or a conspiracy), to claim authority (speaking with boldness like someone who knows the truth is on their side), and forcing the issue (bringing the gospel out of the shadows into the marketplaces).

God desires for His Word to be constantly on our lips, in our lives, and shared openly, proclaimed “from the housetops”, not kept to ourselves. We see this all throughout Scripture: “And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up. And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes. And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates.” (Deut 6:6-9 KJV); “This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success.” (Joshua 1:8 KJV); “My mouth shall shew forth thy righteousness and thy salvation all the day; for I know not the numbers thereof.” (Ps 71:15 KJV); “Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people” (Ps 96:3 KJV); “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.” (Mk 16:15 KJV); “Go, stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life” (Acts 5:20 KJV); “For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.” (Acts 4:20 KJV); “Preach the word; be instant in season(when it’s convenient), out of season(when it’s not convenient); reprove, rebuke, exhort with all long suffering and doctrine.” (2 Tim 4:2 KJV); “Some indeed preach Christ even of envy and strife; and some also of good will: The one preach Christ of contention, not sincerely, supposing to add affliction to my bonds: But the other of love, knowing that I am set for the defence of the gospel. What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice.” (Phil 1:15-18 KJV). Compare this to the Imperial Religion that in the Council of Constantinople of 381AC, it essentially prohibited the discussion of theology. The official Nicene doctrine was fixed. Public dissent or teaching against it was treated as heresy, and heretics could be excommunicated, exiled, barred from church life, or murdered. State-supported “orthodoxy” replaced open pluralism. Today, false religions will attempt to do the same to its congregants. Convincing them that they’re not smart enough or holy enough to study God’s Word on their own. They place human mediators and lifeless statues between them and God’s Word. There is a massive difference between what men say God says, and what God actually says. Scripture commands us to read it daily, so that we may not sin against His Law. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.” (Col 3:16 KJV). The clear biblical pattern shows that God expects His people to hear, read, meditate on, and obey Scripture, and not to treat it as optional or secondary (Jos 1:8; Neh 8:3; Ps 1:1-2; Ps 119:9-10,18,105,130; 2 Tim 3:16-17; Col 3:16; Jn 5:39; Acts 17:11; etc). “Have you not read? - Jesus (Mt 12:3,5; 19:4; 21:16,42; 22:31, etc).

28.x: Jesus is addressing the disciples’ very real fear of being executed by the “wolves” (v.16). The “Them”, the human persecutors, they can end your biological life, but their reach stops at the grave. They cannot touch your eternal identity or your relationship with God. The “Him” refers to God (the Judge). Jesus is saying that if you are going to be concerned about consequences, look toward the One who had jurisdiction over eternity, not just the present moment. Some interpret the word “destroy” (apollumi in Greek) to mean that God simply wipes a sinful soul out of existence (annihilationism). However, a deeper look at the biblical context and the Greek language suggests otherwise. First, in the NT, “apollumi” rarely means “to cease to exist.” It usually means “to be rendered useless” or “to be lost/ruined.” For example, in Mt 9:17, the same word is used when the wineskins “perish” (are destroyed). The wineskins don’t vanish into thin air; they are ruined and can no longer fulfill their purpose. Hence, to “destroy” a soul in Hell is to consign it to a state of eternal ruin where it can no longer fulfill its purpose of glorifying and enjoying God. Jesus specifies the destruction of both body and soul. In the final judgement, the bible teaches a resurrection of both the just and the unjust (Acts 24:15). If the soul were simply “deleted” at death, there would be no body to destroy in Hell later. The fact that the body is included suggests a conscious, physical experience of judgement. Jesus also often describes Hell (Gehenna) using terms that imply ongoing existence rather than a quick end. In Mark 9:48, he describes it as a place where “their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.” If the soul were destroyed (non-existent), the “worm” would have nothing to feast on, and the fire would have nothing to burn. Also, in Matthew 25:46, Jesus contrasts “everlasting punishment” with “eternal life.” Both use the same Greek word for “eternal” (aionios). If the life is consciously forever, the punishment is logically consciously forever. The purpose of the warning is not to describe the mechanics of how a soul dies, but to highlight the authority of the Judge. Jesus is telling his disciples: “Man can only take your life; God can take your eternity.”

29.x: In the 1st-century market, sparrows were the cheapest meat available: the food of the poorest of the poor. A “farthing” (assarion) was a copper coin worth about 1/16th of a daily wage. “Without your Father”: Jesus doesn’t say the sparrow won’t fall; he says it won’t fall apart from the Father’s knowledge and will. God is present and attentive even at the death of the most “insignificant” creature in the market.

30.x: Jesus moves from the “small” (a bird) to the “microscopic” (a hair). To “number” the hairs is more than just knowing the total count; it implies a level of intimate, constant monitoring. If God manages the inventory of something as trivial and dead as a hair, how much more is He managing the life of the person the hair belongs to?

31.x: Your value isn’t based on your social status, your success as an apostle, or whether the “wolves” like you. Your value is intrinsic because you are a child of the Father. Jesus is saying that fear is what happens when we forget our value in God’s eyes. If you calculate the Father’s care correctly, the “wolves” suddenly look very small. But the moment you take God out of the equation, then what would give value to a person? Its productivity? The money it possesses? Its beauty? When you take God out of the equation is when people start to justify things like abortion and euthanasia. Without God, a baby wouldn’t be worth anything: it can’t take care of itself, it produces nothing, it costs money, etc. Without God, women could be rated based on their beauty. A person rating them from 1-10 would not be wrong. However, WITH GOD, we all have intrinsic value as children of God that must be protected at all cost.

32.x: “Confess”: The Greek word is homologeō, which means “to say the same thing” or “to agree.” To confess Jesus is to agree with God’s assessment of Him: that he is the Messiah, the Son of the Living God, God incarnate. “Before Men”: This is the “house top” principle again (v.27). This isn’t a private prayer; it is a public stance taken in the face of the “wolves” and the “councils.” The man Jesus promises to mirror the disciple’s action. If you stand up for him in the earthly “courtroom”, he will stand up for you as your Advocate in the heavenly one before the Father.

33.x: “Deny” means to disown or to say “I do not know him.” It is the opposite of confession. It is usually motivated by the fear of man (the very thing Jessu warned against in v.26 & v.28). If a person values their safety or social standing more than their relationship with Christ, they are effectively choosing a path that excludes them from His kingdom. Jesus is using the language of a witness in a court. In the ancient world, if a witness refused to testify for someone, the judge would assume there was no relationship between them. It is important to remember that this is a general principle, not an unpardonable sin. For example, Peter denied Jesus three times. However, Jesus is describing here the permanent state of the heart. Peter’s denial was a momentary failure of courage; the “denial” Jesus warns about here is a final, settled rejection of him to save one’s own skin. By saying he will confess/deny them “before the Father”, Jesus is reminding the disciples that he is the only bridge to the One who numbers the hairs on their heads. Your standing with the Father is linked directly to your relationship with the Son: “For there is one(heis:singular masculine one) God, and one mediator between God and men, the MAN(not a second god or divine person) Christ Jesus” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV). “Whosoever denieth the Son, the same hath not the Father: he that acknowledgeth the Son hath the Father also.” (1 Jn 2:23 KJV). These verses are not talking about God-the-Son going before God-the-Father to advocate for us. The bible is very clear that God is “heis”, a singular masculine divine person. In Jesus, there are two witnesses (not three) (Jn 8:17-18), the authentic human born of Mary, and the divine Spirit (the Father) (Jn 10:30; 1 Tim 2:5). The two are one: a temple to its spirit, an image to the invisible God. There will be one sitting on the throne under one face and one name (Rev 22:3-4). Isaiah saw Jesus on the Throne (Jn 12:41; Isa 6:1). The glorified human is the one on the Throne: the lamb of God + God under one face and one name. Jesus already completed one sacrifice for ever (Heb 7:27; 9:12; 10:10), he is not in heaven bowing down to the Father doing temple sacrifices interceding for our sins. The very fact that humanity is sitting on the throne is what intercedes for us, the same way the blood of the lamb interceded for the Israelites when the angel of death walked by (Ex 12:7). The blood is not doing intercession through words and actions, rather, its very presence does the “interceding.”

34.x: Jesus clarifies the cost of discipleship: following him is not a path to social comfort or family harmony, it is a path that often leads to painful separation between those who accept the truth and those who don’t. “Think not that I am come to send peace on earth”: Many expected the Messiah to bring immediate, universal political peace. Jesus corrects this. The peace of offers (peace with God) often creates conflict with the world. The “sword” is a metaphor for division. A sword cuts, separates, and divines. Jesus is explaining that his message is so radical (demanding total allegiance) that it acts like a blade, slicing through human relationships where loyalty is divided between the Kingdom and the world.

35.x: In the 1st century, family was the highest loyalty. When a person puts Jesus above their father, mother, or children, it is viewed as a betrayal by the rest of the family. “I am come to set a man at variance against his father..”: Jesus isn’t saying he wants to break families; he is being a realist. When one person commits their life to the radical ethics of the Kingdom and the others do not, friction is inevitable.

36.x: Jesus cites Micah 7:6, a passage that described a time of extreme moral decay in Israel. Jesus is saying that the coming of the Messiah will force a “sorting” of hearts: those who love God’s truth versus those who prefer the status quo.

37.x: Jesus is placing himself above the deepest, most foundational human bonds. He is not saying you must hate your family. In fact, he commands us to love others elsewhere. He is speaking about priority. WHen your family’s desires conflict with Jesus’ commands, you cannot choose the family, or you have effectively chosen them over him.

38.x: To a 1st-century listener, the “cross” was not a piece of jewelry or a religious symbol. It was a Roman instrument of public execution. When Jesus says “take up your cross,” he is calling his disciples to a life of daily surrender. It means you are walking toward a place of death: you have abandoned your own plans, your own reputation, and your own will to follow His Will. To “take your cross” means to take up God’s Will above your own for all of life, in the same way that the cross was the Father’s Will for the Son’s life.

39.x: The paradox of the Christian life: (1) “Findeth his life”: Protecting your comfort, status, and control. Yet you “lose” your true purpose and eternity. (2) “Loseth his life”: Surrenders to Jesus’ Will and mission. You “find” your true purpose and eternal life. This works because if you “find” (secure) your life on your own terms, you are building on a foundation that will eventually fail (death). If you “lose” (give up) your life to Jesus, you are anchoring your identity in the One who conquers death.

40.x: In this verse, Jesus establishes a chain of identity. He is telling the Twelve Apostles that as they go out on their mission, they are not just messengers; they are legal representatives of the King. In the ancient world, there was a concept called the Shaliah. It meant that a person’s messenger was regarded as being the person themselves. If you welcomed the messenger, you were welcoming the sender. Jesus links the disciples to himself, and then he links himself to the Father. Another way to picture this is to see all humanity linking to the only sinless man, which links them to the divine Spirit (the Father). Jesus is the only way to the Father (Jn 14:6; 1 Tim 2:5), if you accept Jesus you accept the Father because the two are one (Jn 10:30; 14:10-11) in a unity composed of humanity & divinity.

41.x: Having established the “Chain of Identity” in v.40, Jesus now explains the “Chain of Reward.” This verse shows that you don’t have to be the one on the “front lines” to share in the spiritual victory of the mission. “In the name of”: This means recognizing the person for who they truly are. If you welcome a prophet because you value the message of God he carries, you are aligning yourself with his work & will share his reward. God views the supporter of the mission as an equal partner with the messenger of the mission. If a prophet faces “wolves” and “councils,” and you provide him with a bed and a meal so he can keep going, God credits his courage and his converts to your account as well.

42.x: “These little ones”: Jesus is likely referring to his disciples, who were “little” in the eyes of the world: uneducated, without social status, and traveling with no money or extra clothes (v.9). “A cup of cold water”: This is the smallest, most basic act of kindness imaginable. In a hot, dry climate, it was necessary but cost the giver almost nothing. “Verily”: When Jesus says “Verily” (Truly or “Amen” in Greek), he is putting his divine stamp of certainty on the promise. No act of service for the Kingdom, no matter how tiny or “behind the scenes,” goes unnoticed by God.

9-10.x: This wasn’t about being “poor” for the sake of it; it was about urgency and trust. If they traveled light, they moved fast. More importantly, they had to rely on the hospitality of the people they served. “The workman is worthy of his meat”: Jesus is establishing that those who give their lives to spiritual service should be supported by the community they serve. “Your purses”: literally “belts.” The fold of the robe or the girdle served the same function as our pockets. A “scrip” was a small bag for holding various articles. “Coats” were the outer robes or tunics that corresponded to the Roman toga. The Greek for “staves” is actually singular, meaning “staff,” agreeing with Luke 9:3.

11-13.x: The “worthy” host refers to someone open to the message of the Kingdom. “Salute it”: this was likely the standard Hebrew greeting, Shalom (Peace). In Jesus’ context, this wasn’t just a “hello”, it was a prophetic blessing of God’s presence. “Let your peace return”: If the household is hostile, the disciples aren’t to argue or beg; they simply withdraw the blessing. Their peace is a gift that cannot stay where it is rejected. Paul also explicitly says his hands are clean from the blood of those who reject the gospel: “Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean: from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles” (Acts 18:6 KJV) & “Wherefore I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men. For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Acts 20:26-27 KJV). The BSB translates it as: “Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all men. For I did not shrink back from declaring to you the whole will of God” (Acts 20:26-27 BSB).

14-15.x: Pious Jews would shake the dust off their feet when returning to Israel from a “Gentile” (pagan) land to show they wanted no part of its impurity. It was a way of showing rejection (Acts 13:51). By telling the disciples to do this to Jewish cities that reject the gospel, Jesus is saying that rejecting the Messiah makes a “holy” city no different than a pagan one. “It shall be more tolerable”: Clearly, there will be different levels of suffering. Likewise there will be different levels of heaven (Mt 6:19-20; 16:27; Rev 22:12; 1 Cor 3:8-15) Sodom and Gomorrah were the biblical benchmarks for wickedness. Jesus claims that cities rejecting the clear evidence of the kingdom (the miracles and the message) are in a more dangerous spiritual state because they have been given more light and rejected it.

21-22.x: Jesus warns that following him will sometimes mean being betrayed by those closest to you. In a culture where family honor and bloodlines were the ultimate social security, this was a terrifying prediction. “Hated of all men”: This isn’t just about local annoyance; it’s about systematic rejection. The world’s values and the Kingdom’s values will clash so violently that the disciple will become an outcast. “Endureth to the end”: The promise is not that you will avoid suffering, but that you will be sustained through it. The one who endures to the end stays faithful despite the betrayal within his family and community. We know we will endure, not because of our own works, but because of our dependence and faith in Jesus working through us: “Being confident of this very thing, that He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Phil 1:6 KJV) & “For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom 8:38-39 KJV). The genuineness & quality of our faith will be tested and made manifest in our “endurance.” The only thing that could separate us from the love of God, is our own free will. The only way to endure till the end is by “abiding” in the True Vine, for without him, we can do nothing (Jn 15:4-5). Jesus warns: “If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned” (Jn 15:6 KJV). Those who “resist the Holy Spirit”, like the Jews of his time (Acts 7:51), will not be saved.

24-25.x: Jesus is helping the disciples lower their expectations. He uses a logical reality check. If the “Head of the House”(Jesus) is slandered, rejected, and called a servant of the devil, the followers shouldn’t expect to be treated better than their teacher. To be treated like Jesus is the ultimate goal of the disciple. If you are being rejected for the same reasons he was, it is proof that you are walking in his footsteps. Jesus is teaching that their identity is not found in their family name or their social reputation, but in their connection to the Master. “Beelzebub” is a derogatory name for the devil, which roughly translates to “Lord of the flies.”
